There are several more philosophical differences between AI and the human brain. For one thing, all human neurons apparently have a taste that corresponds to a brain area. This is never true of an artificial neural net. 

Secondly, all human neurons are essentially the same, if you can obtain the internal state of the same neuron at two different times (which we cannot do), you will find it to be the same. You can do this with artificial neurons.

Thirdly, human brains appear to learn by weakening some connections and strengthening others. While I do not know that this is the only possibility, you can in fact train a neural network with only weak types of signals. 

Certainly in image recognition, artificial brains behave qualitatively differently from human brains. Artificial nets have some difficulty obtaining invariances to the position and scale of a picture, whereas at least in certain ways human beings only see the "object" in front of us, not the image. It could so happen that the eye is the source of invariances; we probably need a better understanding of what happens between the eye and the higher-level portions of the brain. 

It seems that artificial networks trained for object recognition deal poorly with the existence of occlusions, whereas human beings encounter occlusions very easily. When we see an image of an occlusion, we solve it not as a problem but through looking; when you look at a bunch of leaves, you can see that the leaves are separate from one another.

1. Do not seek advice from your friends or relatives to avoid encouraging your desire to divorce.
